title: How Much Does SEO Cost for a Small Business in 2026?
excerpt: Monthly retainers, hourly rates and one-off projects, priced from a survey of 439 SEO providers, plus what moves the number and what we charge.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Cost guide card: monthly, hourly and per-project SEO price bands, beside the title How much does SEO cost for a small business

body.text: SEO is sold three ways: by the month, by the hour and by the project. Each has a market rate, and the rates are better documented than most marketing prices because one large survey asked the people who sell it. This guide uses that survey, explains what moves a quote up or down, and shows where [our SEO and AI search packages](/pricing/marketing-ads) sit.

The survey is [Ahrefs' poll of 439 SEO service providers](https://ahrefs.com/blog/seo-pricing/), who were checked by hand to confirm they really sell SEO. Its headline figure is an average of $2,917 a month, and $1,557 a month for local SEO, which is the closest match for most small businesses. Ahrefs makes SEO software and does not sell SEO services, and the page was last updated in August 2024, so treat the numbers as a recent baseline; this month's market may differ.
The short answer

items: Monthly retainer: $501 to $1,000 a month is the most common band, charged by 20.4% of providers. 68.8% charge $2,000 a month or less.
Local or small business SEO: $1,557 a month on average.
Hourly: $75 to $100 an hour is the most common rate, and the average is $111.
One-off projects: $2,501 to $5,000 is the most common fee, charged by 21.2% of providers.
Who you hire matters: Ahrefs found agencies charge 138% more than freelancers.

body.text: The three pricing models

A retainer buys continuing work: content, on-page changes, reporting and whatever the month needs. 78.2% of the providers in the survey charge this way. It suits a business that competes for the same searches every month and needs someone watching.

A project buys a defined result: an audit, a site migration, a technical clean-up. It suits a site with a known problem, such as pages Google cannot index or a redesign that lost its rankings, and it should end with the problem fixed and documented.

Hourly work suits advice: a second opinion on a plan, or help reading Search Console. Our post on [reading Search Console without chasing noise](/blog/how-to-read-google-search-console-without-chasing-noise) covers what you can do yourself before paying anyone by the hour.
What moves the price

items: How much is broken. A site with no titles, no descriptions and pages blocked from Google needs a fix before anything else will work, and that fix is a project.
How many pages and locations. A five-page site for one town is a different job from a store with two thousand products or a business with ten locations.
How crowded the search is. A medical spa in a competitive suburb faces more and better-funded rivals than a specialist trade in a small town.
Who writes the content. Content is usually the largest ongoing cost. A retainer that includes writing costs more than one that only advises on it.
Paid ads. Some retainers bundle Google and Meta ad management. The ad spend itself is always extra.

body.text: AI search, and what it changes

[Google's guide to AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and that the same foundational SEO practices apply. So most "AI search optimization" is the same work: a site that is fast, crawlable, clearly structured and consistent with your Google Business Profile. Our post on why [AI search still needs a real website](/blog/ai-search-still-needs-a-real-website) explains the overlap.
The cheapest SEO is the problem you fix once: a page Google can finally index stays indexed.
What we charge

items: SEO + GEO Optimization Sprint, $3,500 one-time: a full technical and on-page audit with a written report, then the fixes themselves, including images, meta tags on every page, structured data, AI-crawler access, Google Analytics 4 with conversion tracking, and Core Web Vitals work.

Growth Retainer, $3,000 a month: Google and Meta ad management (spend separate), keyword research and on-page optimization, a quarterly content plan with two blog posts a month, two email campaigns a month, conversion work on key pages, and a monthly strategy call.

body.text: Against the survey, the sprint sits at the top of the most common project band, and it includes the implementation as well as the audit. The retainer is close to the $2,917 overall average, and it covers ad management, email and content alongside the SEO.

The work shows up in measurements a client can check. After our work on [Zahav Medspa](/projects/zahav-medspa), the homepage's average Google position moved from 13.2 to 7.0 across two 28-day Search Console windows, page two to page one, and calls from its Google Business Profile rose 37% from June to August 2026. [Renewed Bodyworks](/projects/renewed-bodyworks) went from no pages Google was allowed to index to nine, and [Florida Green Improvements](/projects/florida-green-improvements) moved from a Lighthouse SEO score of 77 to 100 on every page.
Three example budgets

items: A small site doing most of it yourself: Google Search Console is free, and a few hours of advice at the survey's most common rate of $75 to $100 an hour costs $225 to $300 for three.

A site with a known technical problem, such as pages blocked from Google or a redesign that lost its rankings: a one-time project. Our SEO + GEO Optimization Sprint is $3,500, audit and fixes included.

A business competing for the same local searches every month: a retainer. The survey's local average is $1,557 a month for SEO alone. Our Growth Retainer is $3,000 a month with ad management, email and content included, and ad spend on top.

body.text: Red flags

Google's own guide to [hiring an SEO](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/do-i-need-seo) is blunt: "No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google." It says that if a provider guarantees first place in search results, you should find someone else. Three more questions sort good offers from bad ones.

items: Will you show me every change you make to the site? You should be able to see the work, not only the report.
What will you measure, and where? Search Console and your analytics, with a baseline taken before the work starts.
Who owns the accounts? Your Search Console, analytics and Business Profile should be in your name, with the provider added as a user.

title: How Much Does an AI Chatbot or Automation Cost?
excerpt: Subscriptions, custom builds and the running costs in between. Real prices for chatbots, automation platforms and AI models, and where our packages sit.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Cost guide card: a price ladder from a chatbot subscription to a custom AI build, beside the title How much does an AI chatbot or automation cost

body.text: An AI chatbot can cost $20 a month or $150,000 to build, and both prices are real. The difference is whether you rent a finished product, assemble one from platforms, or pay someone to build it around your business. Each path has a build cost and a running cost, and the running cost is the one most quotes leave vague. This guide prices all of them from published rate cards and shows where [our AI and automation packages](/pricing/ai-development) sit.
Three ways to buy it

items: Rent a chatbot. A subscription tool you train on your site and FAQs. Fast to start, limited to what the vendor built.
Assemble it from platforms. An automation tool such as Zapier or n8n, connected to an AI model and your existing apps. Flexible, and someone has to set it up and keep it running.
Have it built. A custom assistant or agent designed around one process in your business, with its own integrations, guardrails and monitoring.

body.text: Renting: what the subscriptions cost

[Intercom's pricing page](https://www.intercom.com/pricing) charges $19, $85 or $132 per seat a month for its helpdesk plans, plus $0.99 for every outcome its Fin AI agent handles. [Zapier's pricing](https://zapier.com/pricing) includes a chatbot product at $13.33 a month for five bots or $66.67 for twenty, both billed annually.

Vendor surveys of the wider market land in the same place. [Denser, which sells chatbot software](https://denser.ai/blog/how-much-chatbot-cost/), puts a typical small business chatbot at $19 to $89 a month with $0 to $2,000 of setup, and mid-market tools at $100 to $500 a month. Watch the per-outcome fees: at $0.99 each, a thousand Fin outcomes a month add $990 to the bill.
Assembling: what the platforms cost

items: Zapier: free for 100 tasks a month, then plans starting at $19.99 and $69 a month on its pricing page, priced by tasks.
n8n: [cloud plans](https://n8n.io/pricing/) at €20 and €50 a month billed annually, priced by workflow executions, or self-hosted on your own server.
The model itself, billed by usage. [Anthropic's API prices](https://www.anthropic.com/pricing) list Sonnet 5.5 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

body.text: Model usage is usually the smallest line. As a worked example, assume a support conversation sends about 4,000 tokens to the model and gets about 600 back. At the Sonnet 5.5 prices above that is $0.008 in and $0.006 out, about 1.4 cents a conversation, or roughly $14 for a thousand. Your numbers will differ with longer documents or chattier customers, but the order of magnitude holds for most small business use.
Building: what custom work costs

Published ranges for custom builds come mostly from companies that sell chatbots, and they run high. [Quickchat's cost guide](https://quickchat.ai/post/how-much-does-chatbot-cost) puts a typical simple custom bot at $10,000 to $30,000 and a typical custom AI bot at $75,000 to $150,000, with annual maintenance of $5,000 to $15,000. Denser prices each custom API integration at $5,000 to $25,000.

Those figures describe large teams building for large companies. A small business usually needs something narrower: one assistant that knows the business, or one workflow that removes a daily chore. Scoped that tightly, a custom build costs a fraction of those ranges, and the running cost can be lower than a subscription because you pay the model and the server directly.
Price the whole first year: build, platform, model usage, hosting and the hours someone spends keeping it right.
What moves the price

items: How many systems it touches. Answering questions from your website is one job. Reading your calendar, writing to your CRM and emailing a quote is four.
How much it may decide on its own. Every action an agent can take without a person needs guardrails, logging and a way to undo it.
Where your data lives. A subscription keeps your documents on the vendor's servers. A self-hosted build keeps them on yours, at the cost of running a server.
Volume. Per-seat and per-outcome pricing grows with your business. Usage-priced models grow too, usually much more slowly.
Maintenance. Models change, your prices change, your FAQ changes. Someone has to update the assistant, or it starts giving last year's answers.

body.text: What we charge

items: AI Roadmap Sprint, $500: a discovery call, an audit of where AI saves time or money and where it does not, one working proof of concept, and a written roadmap with costs.
AI Assistant, $1,800: an assistant built on Claude or OpenAI and trained on your content, on your site or in Slack or WhatsApp, with guardrails, human handoff, lead capture and 30 days of tuning.

Custom AI Agent, $4,500: an agent built around one business process, integrated with your CRM, calendar, email and forms, self-hosted on a VPS, with logging, a monitoring dashboard and 30 days of support.
Automation Retainer, $750 a month: up to five custom workflows across CRM, ads, email and forms, monitored and maintained.
AI Partner, $1,500 a month: continuous work on assistants, agents and workflows on a self-hosted n8n instance, with one or two new automations shipped a month.

body.text: The one-time builds sit well under the custom ranges vendors publish, because each one is scoped to a single assistant or a single process. The AI Partner plan runs your workflows on a self-hosted n8n instance, so there are no per-task platform fees on top.

Two examples of the narrow kind of system that pays off. [My Challah Dealer's order form](/projects/my-challah-dealer) drops every order into a Google Sheet and sends two emails, a confirmation to the customer and an alert to the owner, with no one copying anything by hand. [Scout](/projects/scout), our own product, polls six listing sources four times a day and scores every listing against a client's profile with the evidence written out, so a person reviews a short list instead of six websites.
Three example budgets

items: Answering the same ten questions on your website: a subscription such as Zapier's chatbot plan at $160 a year, or our AI Assistant at $1,800 once, trained on your own content, plus model usage of about $14 per thousand conversations at the worked example above.

Stopping a daily copy-and-paste job, such as orders into a spreadsheet: an automation platform from $19.99 a month on Zapier or €20 a month on n8n, set up by you or delivered as the working proof of concept in our $500 AI Roadmap Sprint.

Handling new leads end to end, from form to CRM to a first reply: our Custom AI Agent at $4,500, self-hosted on a server you own. If you want us to run that server, our VPS & Self-Hosted care plan is $150 a month, with the server billed at the provider's rate.

body.text: Before you pay for anything

items: Write down the one task you want to stop doing, and how many times a week it happens.
Ask for the full first-year cost: build, platform, model usage, hosting and maintenance hours.
Ask where your documents and customer data will be stored, and who can see them.
Ask what happens when the assistant is unsure: does it hand off to a person, and how?
Ask who updates it when your prices, hours or policies change.

body.text: If the honest answer to the first question is "not often", you may not need AI at all, and a good studio will tell you so. Our post on [AI builds that need business systems](/blog/ai-builds-need-business-systems) goes deeper on that test.

title: How Much Does a Logo and Brand Identity Cost in 2026?
excerpt: A logo can cost $20 or $10,000. What separates a logo from a brand identity, what each price level buys, and where our packages sit.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Cost guide card: a price ladder from a logo maker to a branding agency, beside the title How much does a logo and brand identity cost

body.text: Ask what a logo costs and you will hear numbers from $20 to five figures. Most of that spread comes from one confusion: a logo, a brand identity and a brand system are three different things, and quotes rarely say which one they price. This guide separates them, puts sourced ranges on each, and shows what [our brand identity packages](/pricing/design-branding) include.
Logo, identity, system

items: A logo is the mark: the symbol, the wordmark, or both, delivered as files.
A brand identity adds the pieces that make the mark usable: colors, typefaces, a few rules, and the formats you will actually need.
A brand system goes further: research and positioning, variations for every placement, written guidelines, and the first real applications, from business cards to social templates.

body.text: Each step costs more because each step is more work, and each step solves a different problem. A food truck with one sign needs a logo. A clinic with three locations, a website and a staff of twelve needs a system people can follow without asking.
What the market charges

Two published price sheets agree closely. [Vistaprint's 2026 guide to logo design cost](https://www.vistaprint.com/hub/logo-design-cost) sorts the market into tiers, and [ManyPixels' cost guide](https://www.manypixels.co/blog/brand-design/logo-design-cost-guide), with prices checked in September 2026, lands in the same places. Both companies sell design, so read them as informed vendors' views.

items: DIY and AI logo makers: $0 to $150 on Vistaprint's sheet. ManyPixels puts AI generators at $0 to $30 a month and logo makers at $20 to $200.
Design contests: [99designs' logo packages](https://99designs.com/pricing) run $249, $399, $799 and $1,050, with more concepts at each level and one winning designer.
Entry-level freelancers: $150 to $800 on Vistaprint's sheet.
Experienced freelancers: $800 to $2,500 on Vistaprint's sheet. ManyPixels says most small businesses land between $300 and $2,000.
Design studios and branding agencies: $2,500 to $10,000 or more on Vistaprint's sheet, and $3,000 to $10,000 or more on ManyPixels'.
Large rebrands: $10,000 to $50,000 or more, Vistaprint's premium tier, with deep research and an extensive system.

body.text: What moves the price

items: Discovery. A call and a short brief, or a workshop, a competitor review and a written positioning statement. The second is slower and usually worth it for a business that plans to grow.
Concepts and rounds. Two concepts with one round of refinements is a different job from several directions refined over weeks.
Variations. A primary logo, a stacked version, a small mark for favicons and social avatars, one-color versions for embroidery or stamps. Each one has to work on its own.

Guidelines. A one-page sheet or a fifteen-page guide with spacing, misuse examples and voice. Our post on [brand guidelines small teams actually use](/blog/brand-guidelines-small-teams-actually-use) covers what belongs in one.
Applications. Business cards, signage, packaging, social templates. Designing the logo on real objects is where weak marks get found out.

body.text: Costs nobody quotes

items: Font licences. A typeface found online is not automatically licensed for your website, your packaging or your app. Some licences are per platform. Our post on [choosing fonts for a small business website](/blog/how-to-choose-fonts-for-a-small-business-website) explains what to check.
Trademark search and registration. A designer is not a lawyer. If the name and mark matter to the business, budget for a proper search before you print anything.
Production. Printing, signage, embroidery and packaging cost money on their own, and each vendor wants files in its own format.
File ownership. Make sure you receive editable source files and a written transfer of rights, not only PNGs.

body.text: A good identity is cheap to use: every new flyer, menu or page starts from the system.
What we charge

items: Logo & Style Guide, $750: a discovery call and brief, two or three logo concepts with a round of refinements, final files in every common format, a basic palette and type pairing, and a one-page brand sheet.

Brand Starter Kit, $2,000: a questionnaire and strategy mini-workshop, several logo directions, an expanded palette and type system, a mood board, five to seven social templates, stationery or a business card, and a basic brand guide.

Brand System & Launch, $3,500: a discovery and positioning workshop, a competitive and visual audit, a full logo system, custom palette and type, guidelines of fifteen pages or more, and launch assets such as cards, signage or presentation templates.

body.text: Against the sheets above, the $750 package sits in the entry freelancer tier, the $2,000 kit in the experienced freelancer tier, and the $3,500 system at the low end of the studio and agency range, with a studio's process behind it.

For a sense of what a full system looks like, [My Challah Dealer](/projects/my-challah-dealer) is a one-person home bakery whose identity runs to a badge, a braid mark, two lockups, a wordmark, a die-cut sticker, a bread-clip mark and a six-shape sticker set, with print files for a clip-shaped business card and a bag stamp. [Zahav Medspa](/projects/zahav-medspa) shows the same work at the scale of a medical spa competing for local search.
Three example budgets

items: Testing a side business over a weekend: a logo maker at $20 to $200 on ManyPixels' figures, or a 99designs contest from $249. Expect to redo it if the business works.
A local business about to order a sign and business cards: our Logo & Style Guide at $750, plus the font licence if the chosen face needs one, plus printing. Design once, then print.
A practice with staff, a website and social channels: the Brand System & Launch at $3,500, so everyone who makes a flyer, a post or a slide works from the same guidelines and templates.

body.text: How to choose

items: If you need something this month and the business is still an experiment, a logo maker or a contest is a reasonable start.
If customers already know you and you are about to spend money on a sign, a vehicle wrap or packaging, pay for an identity first. Reprinting is the expensive part.
If more than two people produce materials for the brand, budget for guidelines, or every new flyer will drift a little further.
Whatever you buy, ask for the source files, the font licences and a written rights transfer before the final invoice.

title: How Much Does a Small Business Website Cost in 2026?
excerpt: From a free builder to five figures. What each price buys, what a site costs to run after launch, and where our packages sit in the market.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Cost guide card: a price ladder from a free website builder to an agency build, beside the title How much does a small business website cost

body.text: A small business website can cost nothing or tens of thousands of dollars, and both numbers are honest. The spread comes from who does the work, how much of it is custom, and what the site has to do after someone lands on it. This guide puts real ranges on each option, names where every number comes from, and shows where [our own packages](/pricing/web-development) sit.

The largest published sample is a survey by [WebFX of more than 2,000 businesses](https://www.webfx.com/web-design/pricing/website-costs/). It puts a basic small business site at $0 to $500 with a DIY website builder, and $500 to $5,000 or more when a freelancer or agency designs it. Across every kind of site built by an agency or freelancer, its range runs from $1,000 to $145,000. WebFX sells web design itself, so read those figures as one vendor's view of the market. They are still the best sourced numbers available.
The short answer

items: DIY website builder: free to about $500 a month on WebFX's figures. You do the design, the writing and the setup yourself.
Freelancer or small studio: $500 to $5,000 or more for a small business site, the professional range in the same WebFX survey.
Agency: from about $1,000 into six figures. The top of that range is large custom builds; a five-page brochure site sits near the bottom.
Online store: add the platform. [Shopify's plans](https://www.shopify.com/pricing) run $29, $79 and $299 a month when billed yearly, and its Basic plan charges card fees from 2.9% + 30¢ per sale.
Running the site: hosting, domain, updates and edits. WebFX puts ongoing maintenance from an agency or freelancer at $3,600 to $50,000 a year.

body.text: What actually moves the price
Two quotes for "a website" can differ by ten times and both be fair, because they describe different work. Five things decide most of the gap.

items: Page templates. Ten service pages that share one layout cost far less than ten pages that each need their own design. Ask how many distinct page types the quote covers.
Custom design or a theme. A theme gets you a decent site fast. A custom design is drawn around your business, your content and your customers, and it takes longer to make.
Who writes the words. Copy is easy to leave out of a quote. If you are writing it yourself, the project waits on you; if the studio writes it, that is real work and should be priced.
What the site connects to. Booking, a CRM, payments, a newsletter, a quote form that lands in a spreadsheet. Each connection is a small project with its own testing.
Selling online. A cart, product pages, tax, shipping and checkout turn a website into a store, and the platform fees above start the day it opens.

body.text: The costs that come after launch

The build is the number people compare, and the running cost is the number they live with. WebFX lists the pieces: hosting from $2 to $1,000 a month, and maintenance from $5 to $5,000 a month depending on what is included. That range is wide because "maintenance" means different things to different people.

items: Hosting and the domain: where the site lives and its address. Make sure the domain is registered in your name, whoever pays for it.
Security and updates: plugins, themes and the server itself need patching. A WordPress site that nobody updates is a liability within a year.
Backups: daily or weekly copies you can restore from, tested at least once.
Edits: new photos, a price change, a new service page. Ask how many hours a month the plan covers and what an extra hour costs.
Reporting: a short note on uptime, speed and anything that broke, so you are not the one who finds it.

body.text: Builder, freelancer, studio or agency

A builder makes sense when the budget is close to zero and you have the time to do the work. A freelancer is often the best value for a small site, with the risk that one person is your whole support plan. A small studio sits between: a team you can reach, prices closer to a freelancer's than an agency's, and usually the same people from the first call to launch. An agency earns its fee on large, multi-department projects where coordination is half the work.
Compare what each quote includes, line by line, before you compare the totals.
What we charge

Our prices are published, and each one is a fixed price for a defined scope. Every build is a custom design, and from the Simple Website up the first year of hosting and domain registration is included.

items: Landing Page, $800: one custom page built around a single goal, with SEO essentials and a fast load.
Simple Website, $1,500: up to five pages, a gallery, basic SEO, and a year of hosting and domain registration.
Business Bundle, $2,500: up to ten pages, a content management system, a contact form, Google Analytics, and a year of hosting and domain.
Growth Suite, $5,000: unlimited pages, e-commerce with checkout, a database, custom forms and advanced SEO.
Care plans, $75, $125 or $150 a month: hosting, backups, updates, monitoring and monthly edit hours, from shared hosting to your own server.

body.text: The builds sit inside the $500 to $5,000+ range WebFX reports for a professionally designed small business site. The care plans come to $900 to $1,800 a year, under the $3,600 floor of its maintenance range, because they cover hosting, updates and a few hours of edits, with a fixed scope.

What the money buys shows up in the numbers. When we rebuilt [Florida Green Improvements](/projects/florida-green-improvements), the homepage dropped from 29,834 KiB to 1,839 KiB on mobile and its main content painted in 3.46 seconds instead of 11.62. [Renewed Bodyworks](/projects/renewed-bodyworks) went from a site Google was not allowed to index to nine pages Google can index, listed in a sitemap, with all eight services priced.
Three example budgets

items: A new solo practice that needs to be found and contacted: our Simple Website at $1,500, with the first year of hosting and domain included. From year two, Starter Care at $75 a month, $900 a year, with the domain renewal billed at cost.

A growing service business with a team and a booking flow: the Business Bundle at $2,500, then Growth Care at $125 a month, $1,500 a year, for staging, daily backups and up to three hours of edits a month.

A maker selling online on a platform: Shopify's Basic plan is $29 a month billed yearly, $348 a year, before card fees. At 2.9% + 30¢, a $50 sale pays $1.75 in fees. A designed store on top of that is a build cost, like any other site.

body.text: How to compare two quotes

items: How many distinct page designs does this cover, and what does one more cost?
Who writes the copy, and is that in the price?
Who owns the domain, the code and the content when the project ends?
What is included in the first year of hosting, and what does year two cost?
How fast will the homepage load on a phone, and how will you measure it?
What does a small change cost three months after launch?

body.text: A quote that answers all six in writing is easier to trust than a lower total that answers none. If you want to see the line items for ours, [the Web Development page](/pricing/web-development) lists every package side by side.

title: How to Choose Fonts for a Small Business Website
excerpt: The right website typography is not the trendiest font pairing. It is a small, durable system that makes your business easier to read, recognize, and trust.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Type specimen card with the letters Aa and four Inter weights beside the title How to choose fonts for a small business website

body.text: Choosing website fonts often turns into a tour of whatever looks fashionable this month. That is backwards. A small business does not need a clever type collection. It needs a type system that helps people understand the offer, find the next step, and recognize the business again later.

The font matters, but it is only one part of the decision. Size, weight, line length, spacing, contrast, and loading behavior all affect whether the words feel clear or exhausting. A plain typeface used well will outperform an expressive typeface used without discipline.
Start with the job, not the font library

List the kinds of text the site must handle before opening a font catalog. Most service-business sites need a display style for major headings, a dependable body style, clear labels for navigation and forms, and readable numbers for prices or statistics. An editorial site may need captions and long-form reading styles. A restaurant may need a menu that remains legible on a phone.

This inventory exposes practical requirements. Does the family include a real bold weight? Does it support italics, currency symbols, and every language the business uses? Are the lowercase letters distinct at small sizes? Can someone tell 1, I, and l apart in a booking code or email address? These questions are less glamorous than choosing between geometric and humanist, but customers encounter them.
Use one family well before adding a second

One versatile family is enough for many small-business websites. Hierarchy can come from size, weight, spacing, and placement. That keeps the site coherent and reduces the number of font files the browser must fetch. A second family can add useful contrast, especially when a brand needs a more expressive heading voice, but it should have a defined role.

If two fonts are almost alike, the pairing usually looks accidental. If they are wildly different, the page can feel like two brands arguing. Look for contrast in structure with compatibility in mood. A characterful serif heading can work with a restrained sans serif body. Two decorative faces fighting across every section rarely improve the message.
Typography earns trust when the reader notices the message before noticing the type system.
Build the reading conditions

Do not approve typography from a large desktop mockup alone. Test real paragraphs, form labels, buttons, prices, and error messages on a narrow phone. Body text needs enough size and line height to breathe. Long lines slow the return from one line to the next, while very short lines make the eye jump constantly. A comfortable reading column is a design decision, not leftover space.

Avoid fully justified body copy on the web. It can create uneven gaps between words. Keep contrast strong, and do not depend on an ultra-light weight to make the site feel premium. Thin gray text often looks refined only on the designer's display. On an older phone in daylight, it simply disappears.

Accessibility also means allowing the reader to change the presentation. WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.12 does not require every site to use one prescribed spacing recipe. It requires content and controls to survive when a reader increases line, paragraph, letter, and word spacing. Test that headings wrap, buttons grow, and cards do not clip their contents.
Make hierarchy repeatable

A type system should tell the team what to do next. Define a small scale for the page title, section headings, body copy, supporting text, and interface labels. Give each style a purpose instead of naming it only by appearance. “Service section heading” is easier to apply consistently than “large semibold.”

items: Use the largest style for the page's main idea, not for every sentence someone wants noticed.
Keep body copy consistent across service pages, articles, forms, and policy pages.
Use bold selectively so emphasis still means something.
Treat buttons and navigation as interface text, with clear labels and enough room to wrap or resize.
Test the system with the longest real heading and label, not tidy placeholder copy.

body.text: Check the license and the load

A font found online is not automatically licensed for commercial web use. Record where it came from, what the license permits, and whether the files may be self-hosted. This avoids rebuilding the identity when a client, platform, or vendor asks a basic ownership question.

Then ship only what the site uses. Loading several families, every available weight, and multiple character sets creates cost without improving the design. Modern compressed formats and careful subsetting can help, but they do not excuse an undisciplined system. If the font arrives late, the layout should remain usable while it loads.
A practical approval test

Before approving the type system, open a real service page on a phone. Can you understand the business by scanning the headings? Can you read two paragraphs without zooming? Are the price, phone number, form labels, and primary action obvious? Increase the browser's text size and spacing. Does the layout adapt, or do words vanish behind fixed boxes?

Finally, remove the logo from the page and look again. The typography should still feel consistent with the business: calm or energetic, established or experimental, technical or personal. That is the [brand job](/pricing/design-branding). The rest is usability. Good website typography handles both without making the customer work for either. For an identity and site designed as one system, see [My Challah Dealer](/projects/my-challah-dealer).

title: How We Sell a WordPress Theme With a Stripe Payment Link
excerpt: No store plugin: a Stripe Payment Link, a static thank-you page and one small serverless function that checks the payment before it hands over the zip.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Selling a WordPress theme with one Stripe payment link and one serverless function

body.text: When we released Unhurried Pro, the paid version of [our free WordPress theme](/projects/unhurried), we needed a way to sell one zip file. The usual answers were heavier than the job: a WooCommerce store just to sell a WooCommerce theme, a digital-downloads plugin, or a marketplace that takes a large cut. We wanted something small, cheap to run and easy to reason about.
Here is the setup we ended up with, and the one mistake it was designed to avoid.
The pieces

items: A Stripe Payment Link for the product. Stripe hosts the checkout page, takes the card, calculates sales tax and emails the receipt.
A static thank-you page on our site. After payment, Stripe redirects there and adds the checkout session ID to the address.
One serverless function on Netlify. The Download button calls it with that session ID.
A private GitHub release that holds the zip.

body.text: What the function does

The function takes the session ID and asks Stripe about it. It checks two things: that the payment status is paid, and that the session came from our Unhurried Pro payment link, not from some other product. Only then does it fetch the zip from the private GitHub release and stream it back as a download. Anything else gets a plain message asking the buyer to email us with their receipt number.

The Stripe key it uses is a restricted key that can only read checkout sessions. It cannot create charges, issue refunds or see customers. The GitHub token can only read one private repository. Both live as secret environment variables in Netlify, never in the code.
The mistake it avoids

The first version of the plan was simpler: put the zip in the site's public folder at a hard-to-guess address and redirect buyers there. Then we noticed that our site's code lives in a public GitHub repository. Anything committed there is readable by anyone, including a paid zip at a secret path. The file would have been free to anyone who looked.
So the zip never touches the public repository. The public repo holds only the function's code, which is harmless to read, and the file itself stays in a private release.
What it costs

Stripe's normal card fees, plus a small fee for its automatic tax calculation. There is no plugin licence, no store subscription and no server to maintain; the function runs only when someone clicks Download.
When this setup is not enough

If you sell many products, need licence keys, or want automatic update notices inside WordPress, a dedicated digital-sales platform will serve you better. For one product with an occasional new version, a payment link and a single function is plenty. A new version is a new private release and a one-line change to the function. The same setup for your own product is a small [web development](/pricing/web-development) job.

title: Website Redesign SEO: Keep What Already Works
excerpt: A redesign should improve the site without erasing the search visibility it earned. Keep useful URLs, map every change, and test the launch carefully.
author: Moses Atia Poston
imageAlt: Hand-drawn website wireframe sketches in pale blue lines on a dark blueprint

body.text: A website redesign usually begins with what people can see: a dated layout, unclear messaging, awkward mobile pages, or a visual identity that no longer fits the business. Search visibility is less visible, so it is easy to treat the existing site as a blank canvas. That is how a cleaner website launches with missing pages, broken links, and fewer useful visits from search.

The safer approach is not to freeze the old site. It is to understand what the old site already does well before changing it. A redesign should preserve valuable routes, content, and signals while improving the experience around them. The work starts with an inventory, not a mood board.
Inventory the site before deciding what disappears

Build a list of current URLs using the sitemap, content management system, analytics, Search Console, and a site crawl when one is available. No single source tells the whole story. Analytics can miss pages with little recent traffic. A sitemap can omit old URLs that still receive links. Search Console can reveal pages that appear in search even when they are not prominent in the navigation.

For each important page, note its purpose, target audience, current traffic, useful search queries, backlinks, internal links, and whether it generates inquiries or supports a sale. This separates weak pages from quiet pages that still do a specific job. A service page with modest traffic may be worth protecting if those visits come from people looking for exactly that service.

items: Keep pages that answer a distinct customer need, earn relevant search visibility, or support a conversion path.
Improve pages whose topic is useful but whose copy, layout, or next step is weak.
Combine pages only when they genuinely serve the same intent and the new page covers the useful material.
Remove pages with no continuing purpose, then return a real 404 or 410 when there is no relevant replacement.

body.text: A redesign is not a clean slate. It is a renovation of an asset that already has history.
Keep URLs stable unless a change earns its cost

A new design does not require a new URL structure. If a page still serves the same purpose, keeping its address removes an unnecessary migration step. Shorter or prettier URLs are not automatically better when the existing versions are already indexed, linked, and familiar to customers.

When a URL must change, create a one-to-one map from the old address to the closest relevant new address. Use a server-side permanent redirect, such as a 301 or 308, and point it directly to the final destination. Avoid sending every retired page to the home page. That is unhelpful to visitors and may be interpreted by Google as a soft 404 when the destination does not replace the old content.
Carry the page's meaning into the new design

A page can keep the same URL and still lose its purpose. Redesigns often shorten copy to make a layout feel cleaner, rename headings to sound more branded, or move important details into interactions that are harder to find. The result may look more polished while answering fewer customer questions.

Preserve the substance that made an important page useful: the service description, location context, evidence, frequently asked questions, and a clear next step. Review the title element, main heading, meta description, image text alternatives, canonical URL, and structured data where applicable. These should describe the page that actually launched, not the page that existed in the design file.
Rebuild internal links as part of the architecture

Internal links tell visitors what is related and give search engines paths through the site. A redesign can quietly remove them when navigation changes, old articles are not migrated, or calls to action are replaced with generic buttons. Update links so they point directly to final URLs rather than passing through redirects. Keep important service and location pages reachable through clear navigation or contextual links.

This is also the moment to check link language. “Learn more” repeated across a page reveals little about the destination. A descriptive link such as “[review our web development services](/pricing/web-development)” makes the next step easier to predict. Clarity helps people first, which is a good standard for the architecture as a whole.
Treat staging controls as launch risks

Development sites are often protected with a password, blocked in robots.txt, or marked noindex. Those controls are useful while the site is private and costly when they reach production by mistake: [Renewed Bodyworks](/projects/renewed-bodyworks) arrived with noindex on every page and a site: search that returned nothing. Add crawl and indexing checks to the launch list. Confirm that public pages return successful status codes, canonical tags use the live domain, and the production robots rules do not block sections that should appear in search.

Generate a sitemap with the final public URLs and submit it in Search Console. Keep the existing verification method intact. Test forms, phone links, downloads, analytics, consent settings, and key events on the live site. Search traffic is not useful if the redesigned contact form never delivers the inquiry.
Monitor the launch by page, not by panic

Google notes that search visibility can fluctuate while a site move is crawled and processed. That does not make every decline harmless. Record a pre-launch baseline, then watch important pages, queries, indexed URLs, crawl errors, form submissions, and server logs after launch. Check redirects in batches, not only the five pages someone remembers to open manually.

Separate expected transition from preventable damage. A temporary wobble while changed URLs are processed is different from a service section returning 404 errors or carrying a noindex tag. The first needs observation. The second needs a fix. A redesign succeeds when the new site is clearer, faster, and easier to use without making existing demand start from zero.
